challenges.name: secret-in-client-bundle
challenges.title: Where does the key end up?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the vibe-coded course studio: a key found in the built JavaScript, and the .env file the agent edited. Decide what each one means for who can read the key.

questions.explanation: True. A file under .next/static is served to every browser that loads the page; the grep shows the build wrote the key's value into it, so anyone can find it in DevTools > Sources or in the network response, and copies of that chunk may sit in browser caches, CDNs and screenshots. Moving the call behind a server route stops new builds from shipping it, but the old value has already been published: treat it as leaked, revoke it at the vendor, issue a new key that only the server reads, and check the vendor's usage log for calls you did not make. The misconception is that deleting the line removes the leak.

questions.question:
.gitignore:
.env*.local

.env.local (on the build machine, never committed):
NEXT_PUBLIC_AI_API_KEY=sk-fake-4f9a1c7e2b8d6a0f93e1

Statement: "Because .env.local is git-ignored, the key stays on the build machine and the server, and visitors of the site cannot read it."
questions.explanation: False. .gitignore only keeps the file out of the repository. The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix tells Next.js to copy the variable's value into the JavaScript built for the browser wherever client code reads it, so the value is published with every deploy, whatever file it came from. A variable without the prefix stays on the server, which is where an API key belongs. The misconception is to treat "not in git" as "secret"; the question to ask is which code reads the value and where that code runs.

challenges.name: move-the-api-key-out-of-the-frontend
challenges.title: Vibe-coded app: the AI key in the client bundle
challenges.description: The CodeDev course studio has a "Suggest an outline" button. The coding agent first wrote a server route for it, saw it answer 401 in the demo, removed the session check, and then made the browser call the AI vendor directly with the key in NEXT_PUBLIC_AI_API_KEY. The vendor now reports the key in use from addresses that are not CodeDev's. The file models the app as two modules, marked CLIENT (everything inside the `client` object is bundled and shipped to every browser; the build inlines each `publicEnv.NEXT_PUBLIC_*` it reads) and SERVER (the `server` object, which may read `serverEnv`), plus a fake network and a bundle scanner. Fix both modules so that: (1) client.suggestOutline(title) sends exactly one request, POST /api/outline (the same-origin path, which carries the user's session cookie) with the JSON body {"title": title}, and returns {ok: true, outline} for a 200 or {ok: false, status, error} with the error string of the response otherwise; (2) server.postOutline answers, checked in this order: no user (req.user is null) 401 {"error":"unauthenticated"}; a body that is not JSON or whose title is not a string of 1 to 120 characters after trimming 400 {"error":"invalid_title"}; more than 5 accepted requests by the same user in the same minute 429 {"error":"rate_limited"} (fixed window: Math.floor(clock.now / 60000); each user has their own counter; requests rejected with 401 or 400 do not count); otherwise it calls the AI vendor with the key from serverEnv.AI_API_KEY and the trimmed title as topic (3 sections, as the agent's route already does) and returns 200 {"outline": sections}, or 502 {"error":"upstream_error"} if the vendor fails; (3) no string the browser can reach contains the key: the client must not read publicEnv.NEXT_PUBLIC_AI_API_KEY, serverEnv or ENV, or keep the key in any property. The test runner prints, for each step, the result and the requests the browser sent (a request that carries the key is marked), the bundle scanner's findings when asked, and finally how many AI calls came from the server and from browsers. The hidden tests scan the bundle, call the route without a session and check the per-user limit and invalid titles.
hints: Who should hold the AI key: the code that runs in every visitor's browser, or the code that runs on your server? And once the server makes the call for the browser, who decides which callers it makes it for?

Look at the URL and the headers in client.suggestOutline, and at the first lines of server.postOutline (the comment says what the agent removed). The route also needs a counter per user and per minute before it calls the vendor.

A similar case: a translation button that called https://translate.example/v2 with publicEnv.NEXT_PUBLIC_TRANSLATE_KEY. The fix sends POST /api/translate {"text"} from the browser; the route returns 401 without a user, keeps a counter keyed by the user id and Math.floor(now / 60000) below its limit of 20, and only then reads serverEnv.TRANSLATE_KEY to call the vendor.
